paper_title: YANAMI: A Large-Scale Multimodal Dataset and Benchmark for Multiturn Stateful Interaction

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) integrate visual understanding, generation, and editing within a single unified framework. However, existing unified multimodal datasets and benchmarks remain dominated by single-turn tasks. Even in recent multi-turn datasets, many turns can be solved independently without tracking information across turns. Consequently, they provide limited supervision and evaluation for multimodal stateful interaction, which requires models to understand, maintain, update, and faithfully realize evolving dialogue states across turns. To address this gap, we introduce YANAMI, the first large-scale multimodal dialogue dataset and benchmark for stateful interaction, comprising YANAMI-400K and YANAMI-Bench. YANAMI-400K contains 400K multi-turn multimodal dialogues, with more than 2M images and 2.6M dialogue turns. The dialogues span four representative scenarios: Multi-Image Fusion, Image Editing, World Modeling, and Visual Reasoning, and require models to continuously track, preserve, and revise evolving multimodal dialogue states across turns. YANAMI-Bench comprises 400 multi-turn dialogues for systematically evaluating multimodal stateful interaction. It jointly evaluates Dialogue State Understanding and Visual Realization, characterizing the gap between models' ability to understand evolving dialogue states and their ability to faithfully realize them in visual outputs. Experiments show that fine-tuning BAGEL on YANAMI-400K improves image editing, generation, and multimodal stateful interaction by 10.3%, 2.0%, and 13.23%, respectively, while preserving its general visual understanding capabilities. Evaluations on YANAMI-Bench further reveal that existing UMMs still struggle to maintain, update, and visually realize evolving multimodal dialogue states.

Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) (Deng et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025c; Xie et al., 2026a) represent
an emerging shift from task-specific systems toward unified visual modeling. Unlike conventional
models designed for individual tasks (Liu et al., 2023; Rombach et al., 2022), UMMs integrate image

sections.content: However, most publicly available datasets focus on single-turn tasks (Chen et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2025b). Only few support multi-turn interaction (Chow et al., 2026b; Feng et al., 2026), and even these often contain turns that can be solved independently without tracking information across turns, falling short of complex multi-turn multimodal interaction. In contrast, real-world user-assistant image creation and editing are typically not completed in single step, but instead involve continuous multi-turn stateful interaction for gradual refinement. Here, stateful interaction refers to multi-turn dialogue in which the user and assistant discuss alternatives, make decisions, establish cross-turn constraints and dependencies, plan subsequent steps, and revise previous decisions or requirements in response to user corrections. Consequently, datasets without such interactions provide limited supervision for learning to understand, maintain, update, and faithfully realize evolving multimodal dialogue states across turns. It further limits the exploration of UMMs for complex multi-turn multimodal interaction. For example, as illustrated in Fig. 1, existing multi-turn datasets typically alternate between user instructions and assistant edits, with each turn treated independently and lacking cross-turn contextual dependencies, whereas our dataset captures stateful userassistant interactions in which dialogue states are established, maintained, and updated through ongoing context-dependent exchanges. To address these limitations, we introduce YANAMI, the first large-scale multimodal dialogue dataset and benchmark for stateful interaction, comprising YANAMI-400K and YANAMI-Bench to capture evolving multimodal dialogue states and evaluate models performance across understanding, generation, and editing. YANAMI-400K contains 400K multi-turn multimodal dialogues, comprising more than 2M images and 2.6M dialogue turns in total. To construct genuinely stateful interactions, we explicitly incorporate six key capabilities into each dialogue: 1) Reference Resolution; 2) Context Retrieval; 3) Consistency Maintenance; 4) Spatial and Physical Consistency; 5) Constraint Keeping; and 6) CorrectionBased State Updating. Together, these capabilities make stateful interaction explicit in the data, with each dialogue requiring multimodal states to be continuously tracked, preserved, and revised across turns. To instantiate such stateful interaction in diverse settings, we construct dialogues under four representative scenarios: 1) Multi-Image Fusion; 2) Image Editing; 3) World Modeling; and 4) Visual Reasoning. These scenarios jointly exercise diverse capabilities, spanning visual-state composition, modification, transition, and reasoning. YANAMI-Bench comprises 400 multi-turn dialogues designed to systematically evaluate models ability to track, maintain, and update multimodal dialogue states throughout interactions. Specifically, YANAMI-Bench covers the same four scenarios, including complex understanding, generation, and 2 editing tasks, with each dialogue jointly involving all six key capabilities and requiring their coordinated use throughout the interaction. YANAMI-Bench evaluates models along two complementary dimensions: Dialogue State Understanding (DSU) and Visual Realization (VR). DSU evaluates whether model can infer the currently valid multimodal state from the full interaction history. We assess it through capabilityoriented dialogue-based visual question answering along four dimensions: 1) Reference Resolution; 2) Context Retrieval; 3) Constraint Keeping; and 4) Correction-Based State Updating. VR measures whether the generated images faithfully realize the current dialogue state and is assessed by Visual Quality and State Consistency. Together, these two dimensions provide unified evaluation of stateful multimodal interaction. Our experiments demonstrate that training on YANAMI-400K substantially improves model performance on image generation, image editing, and multi-turn stateful interaction tasks while maintaining general visual understanding capabilities. Meanwhile, evaluations on YANAMI-Bench reveal several key limitations of current models in long-horizon multimodal interactions. We hope that YANAMI provides unified foundation for training and evaluating UMMs toward robust multimodal stateful interaction. In summary, our main contributions are as follows: We introduce YANAMI-400K, the first large-scale multimodal dialogue dataset for stateful interaction across understanding, generation, and editing. It comprises 400K multi-turn dialogues with more than 2M images and 2.6M dialogue turns, providing large-scale supervision for six key capabilities required for stateful interaction. We construct YANAMI-Bench, benchmark of 400 multi-turn dialogues. By jointly evaluating DSU and VR, YANAMI-Bench characterizes the gap between models ability to understand dialogue states and their ability to faithfully realize them in visual outputs. Fine-tuning BAGEL (Deng et al., 2025) on YANAMI-400K yields consistent gains in general image generation and editing, as well as DSU and VR, while preserving general visual understanding capabilities. Results on YANAMI-Bench reveal that existing UMMs still face substantial challenges in maintaining, updating, and visually realizing evolving multimodal dialogue states. 2 related work Unified Multimodal Models aim to integrate visual understanding and generation within shared architecture, providing unified interface for processing and producing multimodal content. Existing UMMs explore diverse architectural paradigms, ranging from unified autoregressive modeling(Team, 2024; Wu et al., 2025b) over multimodal representations to hybrid frameworks that combine autoregressive language modeling with diffusionor flow-based visual generation (Deng et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025c). Existing UMMs have demonstrated increasing capabilities across single-turn multimodal understanding, generation, and editing tasks (Chen et al., 2025d; Cui et al., 2025). However, how well these capabilities extend to multi-turn multimodal dialogues with evolving contextual dependencies remains largely underexplored. Multimodal Data and Benchmarks for Understanding, Generation, and Editing. Existing multimodal datasets primarily provide single-turn supervision for individual capabilities such as understanding (Liu et al., 2023), generation (Brooks et al., 2023), and editing (Yu et al., 2025), with some extending to multi-image settings (Chen et al., 2025c; Li et al., 2025). Recent work has further explored multi-turn interaction through sequential editing and interleaved dialogues (Chow et al., 2026b; Qian et al., 2026; Dai et al., 2026). Meanwhile, existing benchmarks largely evaluate individual capabilities in isolation, including understanding (Fu et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2024b; Li et al., 2023), generation (Ghosh et al., 2023), and editing (Liu et al., 2025). More recent efforts have begun to evaluate unified or interleaved capabilities (Xia et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2026b) and multi-turn settings spanning understanding, editing, generation, and unified multimodal interaction (Liu et al., 2024a; Chen et al., 2025b; Huang et al., 2025; Chow et al., 2026b). However, these datasets and benchmarks can often be approached turn by turn without explicitly tracking evolving information across the dialogue, limiting their ability to support and evaluate truly multimodal stateful interaction. In contrast, YANAMI jointly provides large-scale supervision and systematic evaluation for tracking, updating, and faithfully realizing evolving multimodal 3 dialogue states across turns. The comparison between YANAMI and multimodal datasets is provided in Appendix A.1.

sections.title: 3 YANAMI
sections.content: In this section, we present YANAMI, our dataset and benchmark for multimodal stateful interaction. YANAMI-400K provides large-scale training data, while YANAMI-Bench evaluates models across understanding, generation, and editing. We first describe the data construction process in Sec. 3.1, followed by the evaluation setting and metrics in Sec. 3.2 and the dataset statistics in Sec. 3.3.

sections.title: 3.1 Data Pipeline
sections.content: YANAMI-400K. We construct novel stateful dialogues using visual materials drawn from four existing public datasets (Li et al., 2025; Chow et al., 2026b; Wei et al., 2026b; Chen et al., 2026). Our pipeline, illustrated in Fig. 3, leverages GPT-5.6 Sol (OpenAI, 2026a), Qwen3.7-Plus (Alibaba Cloud, 2026), Gemini 3.1 Pro (Google, 2026b), GPT-Image-2 (OpenAI, 2026b), and Nano Banana 2 (Google, 2026a) for data filtering, dialogue construction, and quality control. Specifically, raw images are filtered into four scenario-specific pools (Fig 3.a) and combined with scenarioand capability-oriented prompts to construct multi-turn multimodal stateful dialogues (Fig 3.b). The resulting dialogues are automatically verified for logical coherence and imagetext consistency, with failed samples iteratively corrected and regenerated. Dialogues that pass verification form YANAMI-400K (Fig 3.c). The constructed dialogues span four representative scenarios: 1) Multi-image fusion, where the assistant integrates multiple userprovided or previously generated images according to the dialogue history; 2) Image editing, where the assistant progressively edits an image while preserving prior modifications and visual consistency; 3) World modeling, where the assistant predicts and renders scene states under specified viewpoint changes or actions; and 4) Visual reasoning, where the assistant generates visual outcomes for proposed hypotheses or solutions to support step-by-step reasoning. To make these interactions genuinely stateful, we incorporate six key state-management capabilities across the four scenarios: (i) Coreference resolution, which grounds context-dependent expressions to the correct textual or visual entities; (ii) Dialogue-history retrieval, which identifies and uses relevant information from previous turns; (iii) Cross-turn consistency, which preserves established visual attributes and prior edits across turns; (iv) Spatial and physical consistency, which maintains plausible geometry, physical relations, and state transitions; (v) Constraint adherence, which consistently follows user-specified requirements and restrictions; and (vi) Correction-based state updating, which incorporates user corrections and replaces outdated information accordingly. For example, Fig. 2 presents representative dialogues across the four scenarios, illustrating how multimodal dialogue states are progressively established, maintained, and updated through the joint use of these capabilities. Additional details of the data collection and representative examples are provided in Appendices and E, respectively. YANAMI-Bench. YANAMI-Bench is constructed with LLM assistance, followed by exhaustive human verification and correction by annotators with graduate-level training in STEM disciplines (Fig 3.d). Throughout data construction, we strictly isolate the benchmark from the training dataset to prevent data leakage; as final safeguard, we compare the SHA-256 hashes of all images across YANAMI-Bench and YANAMI-400K, confirming that no exact duplicates exist between them. It comprises 400 multi-turn dialogues covering the four scenarios described above. The benchmark contains complex instructions that require reasoning over cross-turn context, jointly evaluating models capabilities in ability to track, maintain, and update multimodal dialogue states and translating the understanding of the state into visual implementation.

sections.title: 4.1 YANAMI-Bench
sections.content: Settings. We evaluate 2 close-source models, 4 open-source image editing models, and 9 unified multimodal models on YANAMI-Bench, with the results reported in Table 2. Complete capability-level results for each interaction scenario are provided in Appendix D.2. To isolate models ability to leverage multi-turn dialogue context from error propagation caused by previous generations, we adopt GT-History evaluation setting. For image placement, we consider three configurations depending on the model setup: (1) yes-first, where each image is inserted at its first-mentioned position in the dialogue, (2) yes-front, where all images are placed at the beginning of the input, and (3) concatenate, where all images are concatenated into one image for models that cannot directly process sequential multi-image inputs. Implementation details for the history settings and input organizations are provided in Appendix B.4. Based on the results, we can derive the following key findings: Stateful Multi-Turn Multimodal Interaction Remains Challenging. As shown in Table 2, the best average scores achieved by existing UMMs and open-source image editing models on YANAMI-Bench are only 67.41 and 67.30, respectively, indicating that current models still face substantial challenges in multimodal multi-turn stateful interaction. Further examination across different interaction scenarios reveals clear performance variation, with Visual Reasoning yielding the lowest scores for most evaluated models. In contrast, GPT-Image-2 and Nano Banana 2 achieve average scores of 83.05 and 80.93, respectively, outperforming current open-source models overall and suggesting that noticeable gap remains between openand closed-source models in multimodal multi-turn stateful interaction. Multi-turn Dialogue-State Understanding Remains Challenging. We further find that models struggle not only with generating and editing visual outputs, but also with understanding the current multimodal dialogue state. sections.title: 4.2 Train on YANAMI-400K
sections.content: To validate the effectiveness of YANAMI-400K, we fine-tune BAGEL on our dataset, with detailed training configurations provided in Appendix C. The results demonstrate that YANAMI-400K substantially improves image generation, image editing, and multi-turn multimodal dialogue state modeling, while largely preserving the models general visual understanding capabilities. Fine-tuned BAGEL performances on YANAMI-Bench across four interaction scenarios: (i) Visual Understanding. The fine-tuned BAGEL largely preserves its original general visual understanding capabilities. As shown in Table 4, the model achieves improvements of 4.1% and 0.9% on MMBench and POPE, respectively, while exhibiting only slight decrease on MME-P, indicating that training on YANAMI-400K preserves general visual understanding capability. (ii) Image Generation. As shown in Table 4, the fine-tuned BAGEL improves the overall score on GenEval by 2%, demonstrating that YANAMI-400K enhances the models general image generation capability. (iii) Image Editing. As shown in Table 5, the fine-tuned BAGEL improves the overall score on GEdit-Bench-EN by 10.28%, further demonstrating the effectiveness of YANAMI-400K in enhancing image editing capability. (iv) Multimodal Dialogue Stateful Interaction. As shown in Table 2, the fine-tuned model improves by 13.23% over the original BAGEL on YANAMI-Bench. This result demonstrates that YANAMI-400K not only improves general image generation and editing capabilities, but also substantially enhances the models ability to understand, maintain, update, and visually realize multimodal dialogue states throughout multi-turn interactions.

sections.title: 4.3 Reliability of Judge Usage
sections.content: To assess the reliability of our VLM-as-a-Judge evaluation framework, we conduct human evaluation study involving four expert annotators. Specifically, we sample 100 instances from each of three representative models: BAGEL+YANAMI, Emu3.5, and Nano Banana 2, and collect human ratings for comparison. We compute Pearson correlation coefficients(Benesty et al., 2009) between the scores produced by Qwen-3.8-Flash-Next(Qwen Team, 2026) and the aggregated human ratings, and further compare its evaluations with those produced by GPT-5.6-sol, as shown in Fig. 5. The results show that the correlations between Qwen-3.8-Flash-Next and human ratings consistently exceed 0.80, indicating strong agreement between the VLM judge and human evaluation. Moreover, the scores produced by Qwen-3.8-Flash-Next and GPT-5.6-sol exhibit high cross-VLM correlation, demonstrating strong consistency across different VLM evaluators. These results suggest that our evaluation framework aligns well with human judgments and is robust to the choice of VLM judge.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: This work introduces YANAMI, the first large-scale dataset and benchmark for multimodal stateful interaction across understanding, generation, and editing. YANAMI-400K provides 400K multi-turn dialogues, more than 2M images, and 2.6M dialogue turns across four scenarios and six types of contextual dependency. YANAMI-Bench comprises 400 multi-turn dialogues and jointly evaluates dialogue-state understanding and visual realization. Experiments show that training on YANAMI-400K improves multi-turn contextual understanding, image generation, and image editing while preserving general visual understanding. Evaluations on YANAMI-Bench further show that existing UMMs still struggle to maintain, update, and visually realize dialogue states. YANAMI provides unified foundation for robust multimodal stateful interaction.

sections.title: AI Use Statement
sections.content: LLM-based tools assisted with language polishing, code development, data filtering, dialogue construction, and quality control. As detailed in Appendix A, GPT-5.6 Sol, Qwen3.7-Plus, and Gemini 3.1 Pro were used in the data-construction pipeline, while GPT-Image-2 and Nano Banana 2 supported image generation and repair; Qwen-3.8-Flash-Next was additionally used for automated evaluation under the protocols in Appendix B. All benchmark samples and annotations were manually verified; the authors reviewed AI-assisted writing and code, validated the resulting procedures, and take responsibility for the final content and claims of this work.

sections.title: Ethics Statement
sections.content: YANAMI is intended for research on multimodal stateful interaction and is constructed from existing public datasets and model-generated content. We follow the applicable licenses and usage conditions of the source datasets and models. Automated filtering and human verification are applied to improve data quality. We encourage the research community to use and further develop these resources responsibly.

sections.title: Reproducibility Statement
sections.content: We provide the information needed to reproduce our data construction, training, and evaluation procedures throughout the paper and appendix. The construction pipeline, quality-control process, benchmark annotation procedure, and detailed data statistics are documented in Appendices and A.6. The evaluation protocols, score calculation, history and input formatting, and model-specific inference configurations are described in Appendix B, while the fine-tuning configuration is reported in Appendix C. Complete experimental results and the verbatim VLM-as-a-Judge prompts are provided in Appendices and F, respectively. To further support reproducibility, we will release YANAMI-400K and YANAMI-Bench on Hugging Face and publish the prompts used for data construction and evaluation in public GitHub repository.

Our pipeline leverages GPT-5.6 Sol (OpenAI, 2026a), Qwen3.7-Plus (Alibaba Cloud, 2026), Gemini 3.1 Pro (Google, 2026b), GPT-Image-2 (OpenAI, 2026b), and Nano Banana 2 (Google, 2026a) for data filtering, dialogue construction, and quality control. For this initial quality-control stage, we use large multimodal models with the task-specific prompt reproduced in Appendix A.2. The filter deliberately performs permissive coarse screening: an image is marked as rejected only when severe corruption, generation failure, invalid content, or extremely poor visibility makes it clearly unusable. We apply the filter independently to every image and record the resulting quality labels at the image level. For each image group, if more than half of its images are marked as rejected, we discard the entire group; otherwise, we repair only the rejected images and send the repaired versions through the same filtering process again. Samples that remain invalid after this process are discarded. This procedure supplies diverse visual materials for constructing multi-turn multimodal stateful dialogues involving understanding, generation, and editing, without imposing one-to-one correspondence between source dataset and an interaction scenario.

Do NOT reject an image merely because of: - minor blur or low resolution; - imperfect anatomy or object geometry; - small artifacts; - unrealistic details; - mediocre aesthetics; - imperfect composition, lighting, or colors; - minor text rendering errors; - moderate generation artifacts. **Be permissive. When uncertain, KEEP the image.** Return only the following JSON: ```json { "decision": "KEEP" or "REJECT", "reason": "brief reason" } ``` The resulting YANAMI-400K contains 402,639 dialogues. As shown in Fig. 4, Multi-Image Fusion, Image Editing, World Modeling, and Visual Reasoning account for 36%, 25%, 28%, and 11% of the training dialogues, respectively. We retain this naturally varying training distribution while constructing balanced benchmark with 100 dialogues from each scenario, enabling controlled comparison across scenarios. Complete corpusand scenario-level statistics are provided in Section A.6. A.3 Data Construction After data preparation, each scenario-specific pool is combined with scenarioand capability-oriented prompts to construct multi-turn multimodal stateful dialogues, as illustrated in Fig. 3.b. The complete data-construction prompts are provided in the supplementary material. Within each dialogue, visual observations, textual instructions, and generated or edited images jointly determine how the multimodal dialogue state evolves. The four scenarios instantiate distinct forms of this evolution. 1. Multi-Image Fusion : the assistant integrates multiple user-provided or previously generated images according to the dialogue history. 2. Image Editing : the assistant progressively edits an image while preserving prior modifications and visual consistency. 3. World Modeling : the assistant predicts and renders scene states under specified viewpoint changes or actions. 4. Visual Reasoning : the assistant generates visual outcomes for proposed hypotheses or solutions to support step-by-step reasoning. To make these interactions genuinely stateful, we incorporate six key state-management capabilities across the four scenarios: Coreference Resolution, Dialogue-History Retrieval, Cross-Turn Consistency, Spatial and Physical Consistency, Constraint Adherence, and Correction-Based State Updating. 1. Coreference Resolution grounds context-dependent expressions to the correct textual or visual entities. 2. Dialogue-History Retrieval identifies and uses information relevant to the current request from previous turns. 3. Cross-Turn Consistency preserves established visual attributes and prior edits across turns unless the user explicitly changes them. 4. Spatial and Physical Consistency maintains plausible geometry, physical relations, and state transitions. 5. Constraint Adherence consistently follows user-specified requirements and restrictions. 6. Correction-Based State Updating incorporates user corrections and replaces outdated information accordingly. These capabilities cut across the four scenarios rather than forming fixed one-to-one mapping: multiple capabilities jointly construct and maintain the evolving state within dialogue, and the same capability can occur in different scenarios. Every dialogue in YANAMI-400K involves at least four of the six capabilities, requiring multiple cross-turn dependencies to be exercised jointly within the interaction. A.4 Automatic Verification We apply quality control both before and after data construction, following the pipeline in Fig. 3. During data preparation, model-assisted filtering removes unsuitable visual materials and routes potentially repairable samples back through the preparation process. After data construction, each dialogue is automatically verified for logical coherence and imagetext consistency: the former examines the instructions and state transitions across turns, while the latter checks the visual content against its associated textual context. Failed samples are iteratively corrected or regenerated and then re-verified, while dialogues that pass verification form YANAMI-400K or enter the benchmark-candidate pool. This iterative process is intended to eliminate inconsistent state transitions, mismatched imagetext pairs, and dialogues that do not realize the intended scenario or contextual dependencies. A.5 Human Verification and Benchmark Construction We construct YANAMI-Bench with LLM assistance from candidates that pass automatic verification, followed by exhaustive human verification and correction. The benchmark is balanced across the four interaction scenarios, with 100 dialogues per scenario and 400 dialogues in total. (i) Dialogue-state understanding QA pairs. Each benchmark dialogue includes four QA pairs, one each for Reference Resolution, Context Retrieval, Constraint Tracking, and Correction Updating. (ii) Fine-grained atomic criteria. Each dialogue also includes atomic criteria for evaluating State Consistency in generated or edited visual outputs. These atomic criteria decompose the requirements of target image into independently verifiable checks, allowing State Consistency to be assessed separately from holistic Visual Quality. As shown in the human-verification stage of Fig. 3, the initial atomic checks are generated with LLM assistance and then reviewed together with the corresponding dialogue and visual content. Three human annotators with graduate-level training in STEM disciplines verify each sample. They inspect the dialogue logic, visual evidence, understanding questions, and atomic evaluation criteria, and correct samples that do not faithfully represent the intended state evolution or evaluation target. Failed samples undergo manual correction or regeneration followed by another review, and every sample retained in the final benchmark is manually verified. The final benchmark contains 1,600 understanding questions and 8,467 atomic visual checks, with detailed per-scenario statistics reported in Table 8. For each generated image, the evaluator compares the candidate with the ground-truth target and assigns binary outcome to every atomic check. check receives credit only when all of its required conditions are visibly satisfied; semantically equivalent visual realizations are accepted when they do not alter the evaluated state property. The State Consistency score is the fraction of atomic checks that receive credit. Capability-specific checks are evaluated separately and are used only for analyses that require alignment between an understanding item and its corresponding generated outcome. Visual Quality assesses the generated image independently of task correctness on 010 integer scale. The rubric considers structural coherence, visual fidelity, generation artifacts, and overall naturalness, with higher scores indicating better perceptual quality. The complete prompts for all three evaluators are reproduced in Appendix F. B.3 Score Calculation For each interaction scenario, we first compute the dialogue-state understanding score as the arithmetic mean of the four understanding metrics: Reference Resolution (RR), Context Retrieval (CR), Constraint Tracking (CT), and Correction Updating (CU). Specifically, the understanding score is calculated as Sunderstanding = SRR + SCR + SCT + SCU 4 . (1) Before aggregation, all component scores are converted to 0100 scale: the State Consistency (SC) score, originally expressed as fraction, is multiplied by 100, and the Visual Quality (VQ) score, originally measured on 010 scale, is multiplied by 10. For models with both understanding and generation capabilities, the final score for each scenario is computed using 4:4:2 weighting over dialogue-state understanding, State Consistency, and Visual Quality: Sscene = 0.4Sunderstanding + 0.4SSC + 0.2SVQ. (2) For models without dialogue-state understanding capabilities, the scenario score is computed from State Consistency and Visual Quality using 6:4 weighting: Sscene = 0.6SSC + 0.4SVQ. (3) This weighting ensures that state faithfulness remains the primary component of the final score while retaining an explicit assessment of perceptual visual quality. B.4 History and Input Formatting Our main evaluation adopts the GT-History setting to measure the models ability to use accumulated dialogue state without conflating it with errors produced in earlier generation turns. When evaluating target generation or editing turn, we retain the complete textual dialogue preceding that turn and replace all earlier assistant-generated images with their corresponding ground-truth images. User-provided reference images remain unchanged. The target output itself is never included in the input context. We additionally evaluate Self-History to approximate realistic multi-turn deployment. Under this setting, each image produced by the evaluated model is inserted into the dialogue history and used as visual context for subsequent turns, while the textual history remains unchanged. User-provided reference images again remain unchanged. Consequently, errors in earlier visual outputs may alter the context available at later turns and accumulate throughout the interaction. We use three input organizations according to the interfaces supported by individual models. For interleaved imagetext input, denoted as yes-first, each image is inserted at the position of its first mention in the dialogue, preserving the original temporal order of the interaction. For image-first input, denoted as yes-front, all visual inputs available at the target turn are placed before the textual dialogue in their order of appearance. For models that cannot process sequential multi-image inputs, the available images are concatenated in dialogue order into single composite visual input and supplied together with the corresponding textual instruction. sections.title: C Training Details
sections.content: We fine-tune BAGEL-7B-MoT on YANAMI-400K using NVIDIA A800 and A100 GPUs, each with 80 GB of memory. Our compute resources comprise six-GPU A800 configuration and 16-GPU A100 configuration; the provided launch configuration uses six processes on single node. We employ fully sharded data parallelism (FSDP) under the FULL_SHARD strategy. The model uses Qwen2MoTDecoderLayer and is initialized from the Hugging Face checkpoint and its exponential moving average weights, with only model parameters restored. We jointly optimize visual generation and visual understanding objectives. The VAE is frozen, whereas the language model, vision encoder, and understanding module remain trainable. We use constant learning rate of 1 105 with 100 warm-up steps, cross-entropy loss weight of 0.25, an MSE loss weight of 1.0, gradient accumulation of 1, and maximum gradient norm of 1.0. The expected token count is 12,288, while both the overall and per-sample maximum token counts are 16,384. The maximum latent size is 64, and FlexAttention is enabled. Data loading uses one worker per process and prefetch factor of 2.

sections.title: E Additional Qualitative Examples
sections.content: Figures 811 provide one complete dialogue from each scenario at larger scale. Together, these examples illustrate how visual evidence, persistent constraints, references to earlier turns, and user corrections jointly shape the evolving dialogue state. 28 Figure 8: Complete qualitative example for Image Editing. Across seven turns, the dialogue progressively replaces and modifies visual elements while preserving the active appearance constraints, incorporating user correction, and retrieving earlier requirements for the final composition. The left and right panels show the first and second halves of the same dialogue, respectively. 29 Figure 9: Complete qualitative example for Multi-Image Fusion. The dialogue combines information from multiple visual references while tracking the intended setting, object placement, and persistent restrictions, culminating in jointly composed visual output. The left and right panels show the first and second halves of the same dialogue, respectively. Figure 10: Complete qualitative example for World Modeling. The interaction requires the model to maintain the scene layout, update an initially incorrect depth relation, and render new viewpoint while preserving the corrected spatial state and other persistent scene properties. The left and right panels show the first and second halves of the same dialogue, respectively. 31 Figure 11: Complete qualitative example for Visual Reasoning. The model follows multi-step action plan, revises the plan after user correction, generates intermediate visual states, and subsequently retrieves those states to describe the completed sequence. The left and right panels show the first and second halves of the same dialogue, respectively. 32 VLM-as-a-Judge Prompt Templates We use three task-specific prompts to evaluate dialogue-state understanding, State Consistency, and Visual Quality. sections.title: Prompt for Visual Quality Evaluation
sections.content: You are strict and professional evaluator specializing in perceptual quality assessment of (cid:44) AI-generated images. You will be given: 1. **Generated Image**: an AI-generated image to evaluate ## Your Objective Evaluate the **perceptual quality** of the AI-generated image, focusing on technical excellence, visual (cid:44) coherence, and absence of generation artifacts. ## Quality Assessment Dimensions ### Structural Coherence - **Anatomy/Geometry**: Correct proportions, realistic structures, proper object shapes - **Spatial Relationships**: Logical positioning, appropriate scale relationships - **Compositional Logic**: Coherent scene layout, proper perspective ### Visual Fidelity - **Texture Quality**: Realistic surface textures, appropriate material appearance - **Detail Clarity**: Sharp important details, appropriate level of detail throughout - **Color Accuracy**: Natural color distribution, proper lighting/shadow ### Generation Artifacts - **Duplication Issues**: Repeated elements, phantom objects, merged features - **Blending Problems**: Unnatural transitions, ghosting effects, edge artifacts - **Distortion Errors**: Warped features, impossible geometries, scale inconsistencies ### Overall Naturalness - **Photorealism**: Does the image look natural and believable? - **Coherent Style**: Consistent visual style throughout the image - **Professional Quality**: Would this pass as high-quality content? ## Evaluation Scale (0 to 10) impression perfect technical excellence and photorealistic quality - **9-10 Exceptional Quality**: **Professional-grade image** with **no noticeable artifacts or flaws**; (cid:44) - **7-8 Very Good Quality**: **High-quality image** with **minimal flaws** that don't affect overall (cid:44) - **5-6 Good Quality**: **Decent image** with **some noticeable flaws** but overall usable - **3-4 Fair Quality**: **Multiple noticeable flaws** that somewhat detract from image usability - **1-2 Poor Quality**: **Multiple significant flaws** that severely detract from image usability - **0 Unusable Quality**: **Major structural problems**, severe artifacts, completely unusable ## Important Note If the input is composite of multiple images (collage, grid, multiple separate images combined) rather (cid:44) than single coherent image, the maximum possible score is 4, regardless of quality. ## Reasoning Steps 1. **Image Type Assessment**: Determine if this is single image or composite of multiple images 2. **Structural Analysis**: Assess geometric and anatomical correctness 3. **Fidelity Evaluation**: Check texture, detail, and color quality 4. **Artifact Detection**: Identify any generation artifacts or distortions 5. **Naturalness Assessment**: Evaluate overall believability and professional quality ## Input <image> ## Output Format You must return your evaluation as JSON object with the following structure: ```json { } ``` "score": 0-10, "reason":"Simple explanation of your assessment" Note: The score must be an integer value between 0 and 10.

sections.title: G Limitations
sections.content: The current version of YANAMI focuses on four representative interaction scenarios and six core statemanagement capabilities to provide controlled foundation for studying multimodal stateful interaction. While these settings cover diverse forms of understanding, generation, and editing, future extensions may naturally incorporate additional application domains, languages, modalities, and longer interaction It would also be valuable to complement the current controlled evaluation with broader horizons. interactive studies and to examine the benefits of YANAMI-400K across additional unified multimodal model architectures. These directions would further broaden the scope of YANAMI without changing the findings established under the settings studied in this work.
